questions.enonce_markdown:
Show how Paul clarified the doubts of the Corinthians on the question of the resurrection.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Some Corinthians said that there is no resurrection of the dead (1 Corinthians 15:12). Many people in the Greek world believed that the soul is immortal but that the body is a prison to be left behind, and so the idea of a bodily resurrection seemed strange or foolish. In 1 Corinthians 15 Paul answers these doubts in a careful sequence of arguments.

**1. The tradition they had received (1 Corinthians 15:1-11).** Paul reminds them of the Gospel he preached and which they accepted: Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, was buried, was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures, and appeared to Cephas, then to the Twelve, then to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom were still alive, then to James, to all the apostles, and last of all to Paul himself. Resurrection is therefore not a theory but part of the original Christian message, supported by many witnesses.

**2. The logical consequences of denying the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:12-19).** If the dead are not raised, then Christ has not been raised, the preaching is in vain, faith is in vain, the witnesses are false, believers are still in their sins and those who have died in Christ have perished. If the hope is for this life only, Christians are of all people the most to be pitied. Paul shows that denial of the general resurrection destroys the Gospel itself.

**3. Christ the first fruits (1 Corinthians 15:20-28).** Christ has been raised as the "first fruits of those who have fallen asleep". As death came through Adam, so life comes through Christ. In the end death, the last enemy, will be destroyed and God will be all in all. The resurrection of Christ guarantees the resurrection of believers.

**4. Practical arguments (1 Corinthians 15:29-34).** Paul refers to the practice of baptism on behalf of the dead (a difficult verse), to his own daily dangers, and to the saying "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die", which he rejects. If there is no resurrection, there is no reason for his sufferings. He warns that bad company ruins good morals.

**5. The nature of the resurrection body (1 Corinthians 15:35-49).** To the question "How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?" Paul replies with the analogy of a seed that must die before it grows into a plant with a different body. He points to the variety of bodies in creation, and says that the body is sown perishable and raised imperishable, sown in dishonour and raised in glory, sown a natural body and raised a spiritual body. As we have borne the image of the man of dust (Adam), we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven (Christ).

**6. The mystery and the victory (1 Corinthians 15:50-58).** "Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God." At the last trumpet the dead will be raised imperishable and the living will be changed. Death is swallowed up in victory. Paul closes with thanks to God who gives the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ, and with a practical call to be steadfast and to abound in the work of the Lord.

**Conclusion.** Paul clarified the doubts by appealing to the tradition and the witnesses, showing the logical consequences of denial, linking the resurrection of believers with that of Christ, explaining the nature of the risen body and promising final victory over death. His answer made the resurrection the foundation of Christian faith and hope.
